w: Henry VIII founded Trinity in 1546, and it has stayed the richest college at either Oxford or Cambridge since. Great Court, its centerpiece, is reckoned the largest enclosed courtyard in Europe. Isaac Newton worked here, as did Byron and Bertrand Russell - whom the college expelled in wartime, then quietly took back.
_facts: Founded 1546 by King Henry VIII, largest financial endowment of any Oxford or Cambridge college
Great Court said to be the largest enclosed courtyard in Europe
alumni include Isaac Newton, Lord Byron, Vladimir Nabokov, Bertrand Russell (expelled by the college, then reaccepted), six British prime ministers

w: Jesus College rose in 1496 on a dissolved Benedictine nunnery, handed over by the Bishop of Ely, John Alcock - whose surname gave the college its cockerel emblem. From 1560 to 1860 it trained Church of England clergy. In 2019, Sonita Alleyne became its master, the first Black head of any Oxbridge college.
s: A Tudor college built on a dissolved nunnery
_facts: Established 1496 on site of the 12th-century Benedictine nunnery of St Mary and St Radegund by John Alcock, Bishop of Ely
cockerel symbol derives from founder's surname
was primarily a clergy training college from 1560 to 1860
Sonita Alleyne elected master in 2019, first Black leader of an Oxbridge college

w: Henry VI founded King's College in 1441, soon after founding Eton, and for decades it admitted only Eton boys. War and the king's own downfall stalled its chapel for decades; it wasn't finished until 1544, under Henry VIII. Every Christmas Eve, the college choir broadcasts Nine Lessons and Carols to millions worldwide.
s: Henry VI's royal foundation, feeding straight from Eton
_facts: Founded 1441 by King Henry VI shortly after he founded Eton College, initially accepted only Eton students
chapel construction began 1446, finished 1544 under Henry VIII
Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols broadcast from the chapel every Christmas Eve to millions worldwide

w: Chartered by the Tudor matriarch Lady Margaret Beaufort in 1511, St John's grew into one of Cambridge's largest colleges, second-wealthiest after Trinity. Its alumni include the poet Wordsworth and, more consequentially, William Wilberforce and Thomas Clarkson, who led the fight that ended British slavery.
s: Where two men who ended the slave trade once studied
_facts: Founded by Lady Margaret Beaufort, charter dated 9 April 1511
one of the largest Oxbridge colleges by student numbers, second-wealthiest at Oxford/Cambridge after Trinity
alumni include William Wordsworth, William Wilberforce and Thomas Clarkson, twelve Nobel Prize winners and seven prime ministers

w: Newnham grew out of an 1871 scheme called Lectures for Ladies, organised by philosopher Henry Sidgwick and suffragist campaigner Millicent Garrett Fawcett, at a university that wouldn't yet award women degrees. It became Cambridge's second women's college, after Girton, marking 150 years across 2021 and 2022.
s: Born from a suffragist's Lectures for Ladies
_facts: Founded 1871 by a group organising Lectures for Ladies, including Henry Sidgwick and Millicent Garrett Fawcett
second women's college founded at Cambridge, after Girton
celebrated 150th anniversary through 2021-2022

w: Christ's College began in 1437 as the plainly named God's House, until Lady Margaret Beaufort's 1505 endowment rebuilt it as Christ's, the twelfth college founded at Cambridge. Its alumni include the poet John Milton and the naturalist Charles Darwin, alongside a run of Nobel Laureates who came much later.
s: God's House, refounded for Milton and Darwin
_facts: Founded by William Byngham in 1437 as God's House
granted new royal charter and substantial endowment from Lady Margaret Beaufort in 1505, renamed Christ's College, twelfth Cambridge college founded
alumni include John Milton, Charles Darwin, and Nobel Laureates Martin Evans, James Meade, Alexander Todd, Duncan Haldane, John Clarke

w: Emily Davies and Barbara Bodichon founded Girton in 1869 as Cambridge's first women's college, set two miles out of town, red-brick and Victorian, designed by Alfred Waterhouse. It took until 1948 for the university to grant it full college status, officially admitting women. Alumnae include Queen Margrethe II.
s: The women's college that forced Cambridge's hand
_facts: Established 1869 by Emily Davies and Barbara Bodichon as Cambridge's first women's college
granted full college status in 1948, marking official admittance of women to the university
first Cambridge women's college to become coeducational, in 1976
main site about 2.5 miles northwest of the city, 50 acres, Victorian red-brick built by Alfred Waterhouse 1872-1887
alumnae include Queen Margrethe II, Lady Hale, Arianna Huffington, Sandi Toksvig

w: Pembroke is Cambridge's third-oldest college, buildings stacked century by century since the Middle Ages, and it holds Christopher Wren's first finished work: the chapel, his debut before St Paul's. It also educated William Pitt the Younger, and its library keeps an original first encyclopaedia with printed diagrams.
s: Wren's first chapel, and Pitt the Younger's college
_facts: Third-oldest college of the university, buildings from almost every century since founding
contains the first chapel designed by Sir Christopher Wren
one of only six Cambridge colleges to have educated a British prime minister - William Pitt the Younger
library holds an original copy of the first encyclopaedia to contain printed diagrams

w: King's College Chapel took seventy years to finish, spanning the Wars of the Roses and outlasting the kings who started it. What emerged ranks among the finest late Gothic buildings in England, crowned by the largest fan vault in the world - still active as worship, and Cambridge's defining silhouette.
s: The world's largest fan vault, built through civil war
_facts: Built in phases from 1446 to 1515, spanning the Wars of the Roses and three decades
considered one of the finest examples of late Perpendicular Gothic English architecture, with the world's largest fan vault
stained-glass windows completed by 1531, rood screen erected 1532-36
active house of worship and home of the King's College Choir; a landmark symbol of the city

w: While every other old Cambridge college traces to a bishop, king or wealthy patron, Corpus Christi was founded in 1352 by two guilds of townspeople - the only college with that distinction. Long known as Bene't College, it stayed small and grew rich in silver plate, punching above its numbers academically.
s: Founded by the town, not the crown
_facts: Founded 1352 by the Guild of Corpus Christi and the Guild of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the only college founded by Cambridge townspeople
commonly known as Bene't College from the late 14th to early 19th century
one of the smallest student bodies among traditional colleges, exceptionally rich in silver, endowment £99.7m in 2023
ranked third in the Tompkins Table in 2024

w: Margaret of Anjou founded Queens' in 1448, and its buildings still straddle the Cam, the two halves stitched together by the Mathematical Bridge. Erasmus lodged here on his visits to England in the early 1500s, centuries before alumnus Demis Hassabis took the college's first Nobel Prize, in 2024, for AI work.
_facts: One of the 16 "old colleges" of Cambridge, founded 1448 by Margaret of Anjou
buildings span the River Cam, connected by the Mathematical Bridge and Silver Street
Desiderius Erasmus studied here during visits to England 1506-1515
alumnus Demis Hassabis won the college's first Nobel Prize in 2024 for AI work

w: Founded in 1473 as Katharine Hall, renamed St Catharine's in 1860, this college - nicknamed Catz - breaks convention with an open court facing Trumpington Street instead of a closed quadrangle. Wedged between King's College and Corpus Christi, it runs a tight community of about a thousand students, fellows and staff.
s: The college with an open court, not a closed quad
_facts: Founded 1473 as Katharine Hall, took current name in 1860, nicknamed "Catz"
located in historic city centre, just south of King's College and across from Corpus Christi
notable for an open court facing Trumpington Street rather than a closed quadrangle
community of approximately 1000 fellows, students and staff

w: It looks like a curved arch spanning the Cam, but the Mathematical Bridge is built entirely from straight timbers, arranged by William Etheridge in 1749 into a design that only reads as a curve from a distance. It has been rebuilt twice since, in 1866 and 1905, and a replica crosses the water near Oxford's Iffley Lock.
s: The arch that's secretly built from straight timbers
_facts: Wooden footbridge connecting two parts of Queens' College across the River Cam, officially the Wooden Bridge or Queens' Bridge
designed by William Etheridge, built by James Essex in 1749, Grade II listed
appears to be an arch but is composed entirely of straight timbers, an unusually sophisticated engineering design, hence the name
rebuilt in 1866 and 1905 keeping the same design
a replica was built in 1923 near the Iffley Lock in Oxford

w: The Eagle opened as a coaching inn in 1667, though its frontage dates to around 1600, making it the second-oldest pub in Cambridge after the Pickerel Inn. A galleried Victorian wing wraps its courtyard behind. Ownership never left academic hands: Corpus Christi College still owns the site, Greene King running the taps.
s: Cambridge's second-oldest pub, still owned by a college
_facts: Formerly the Eagle and Child, Grade II listed pub, opened 1667 as a coaching inn
second-oldest pub in Cambridge after the Pickerel Inn
front dates to circa 1600, with a galleried 19th-century wing facing the courtyard
site owned by Corpus Christi College, pub managed by Greene King brewery

w: John Stevens Henslow, the botanist who mentored a young Charles Darwin, created this forty-acre garden in 1831, opening it to the public in 1846. It now holds past eight thousand plant species, and in July 2019 recorded the second-highest UK temperature ever, 38.7C, since briefly beaten.
s: Darwin's mentor planted this heat-record-setting garden
_facts: Created 1831 by Professor John Stevens Henslow, Charles Darwin's mentor, opened to the public in 1846
covers 16 hectares (40 acres), holds over 8,000 plant species
recorded the second-highest UK temperature ever, 38.7C, on 25 July 2019
on 19 July 2022 reached 39.9C, the same day the UK record was broken at Coningsby, Lincolnshire

n: Church of St Mary the Great
w: Great St Mary's is Cambridge's university church, so central to academic life its rules once required officers to live within twenty miles, undergraduates within three. Its clock chimes a sequence called the Cambridge Quarters - the same melody later borrowed for the Houses of Parliament's Big Ben, written here first.
s: The clock chimes that became Big Ben's tune
_facts: Church of England parish church and the university church for the University of Cambridge, Grade I listed
at the north end of King's Parade, known locally as Great St Mary's or GSM
university legislation requires officers to live within 20 miles and undergraduates within 3 miles of it
houses the University Clock, whose chimes (the Cambridge Quarters) were later used by the clock tower of the Houses of Parliament, Big Ben
